claim: Nutrition is a crucial factor for public health.
source: Nutrition is a crucial factor for public health (Afshin et al., 2019; The National Academies of Sciences and Engineering and Medicine Health, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Afshin et al., 2019 and The National Academies of Sciences and Engineering and Medicine Health, 2017

claim: Nutrition research still relies mostly on self-reported dietary information and limited food composition data to investigate the links between health and nutrition.
source: However, despite considerable methodological progress, nutrition research still relies mostly on self-reported dietary information and limited food composition data to investigate the links between health and nutrition.
evidence: Statement about current practices in nutrition research based on established knowledge of the field

claim: Food composition data allows estimation of the intake of specific nutrients and other dietary compounds.
source: Indeed, food composition data is the bedrock on which nutrition research rests today: it allows us to estimate the intake of speciﬁc nutrients and other dietary compounds, and thus enables investigations into the associations between nutrient intake and health outcomes.
evidence: Statement about the function and use of food composition data in nutrition research

claim: Multiple factors affect the ultimate nutrient content of foods, including cultivar or breed, climate, growing and harvest conditions, storage, processing, and methods of culinary preparation.
source: Multiple factors aﬀect the ultimate nutrient content of foods, including cultivar or breed, climate, growing and harvest conditions, storage, processing, and methods of culinary preparation (Greenﬁeld and Southgate, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Greenfield and Southgate, 2003

claim: Apples harvested at the same time from the same tree show more than a twofold difference in the amount of many micronutrients.
source: Even apples harvested at the same time from the self-same tree show more than a twofold diﬀerence in the amount of many micronutrients (Wilkinson and Perring, 1961).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wilkinson and Perring, 1961

claim: Processed foods are usually not standardised for composition but taste, texture, and consumer preferences, and thus vary in their chemical composition.
source: Moreover, processed foods are usually not standardised for composition but taste, texture, and consumer preferences, and thus vary in their chemical composition.
evidence: Statement about food industry practices based on established knowledge

claim: Food composition data are generally used by relying on single-point estimates, the mean food composition, assuming that foods have a consistent composition.
source: Despite all these eﬀorts, food composition data are generally used by relying on single-point estimates, the mean food composition, de facto assuming that foods have a consistent composition.
evidence: Statement about current practices in nutrition research

claim: Self-reported dietary data carry substantial bias.
source: This approach introduces a considerable degree of error, bias, and uncertainty – and these are exacerbated by the limitations of self-reported dietary data which are known to carry substantial bias (Subar et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Subar et al., 2015

claim: Current approaches assume that intake directly correlates with the systemic presence of a given nutrient.
source: Moreover, current approaches also assume that intake directly correlates with the systemic presence of a given nutrient as it is through their systemic presence that many nutrients mediate much of their health-related biological eﬀects.
evidence: Statement about assumptions in current nutrition research approaches

claim: The impact of food composition variability on both the interpretation of research findings and the development of dietary guidance has been largely neglected.
source: While all of this is well known in the nutrition expert community (Gibney et al., 2020), the impact on both the interpretation of research ﬁndings and the development of dietary guidance and advice has been largely neglected, and there are only limited data exploring the impact on research outcomes (Kipnis et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gibney et al., 2020 and Kipnis et al., 2002

claim: These limitations are a key contributor to the inconsistent and often contradictory outcomes of nutrition research and dietary guidance.
source: It seems to be tenable that these limitations are a key contributor to the inconsistent and often contradictory outcomes of nutrition research and dietary guidance, which have received a high level of public attention and signiﬁcant criticism in recent years (Ioannidis, 2018).
evidence: Speculative statement supported by citation to Ioannidis, 2018

claim: The EPIC Norfolk study has detailed dietary data based on the combination of self-reporting and food composition data, nutritional biomarkers, and health endpoints collected at the same time.
source: The European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition (EPIC) Norfolk study (n = 25,618, data available for 18,684; Day et al., 1999) is ideally suited to investigate the impact of the variability in bioactive content on nutritional research because it has detailed dietary data based on the combination of self-reporting and food composition data, nutritional biomarkers, as well as health endpoints collected at the same time.
evidence: Description of the EPIC Norfolk study characteristics, supported by citation to Day et al., 1999

claim: Bioactives are food constituents that are not considered essential to human life but can affect health.
source: Bioactives are food constituents that are not considered essential to human life but can aﬀect health and are therefore extensively investigated (Ottaviani et al., 2022).
evidence: Definition supported by citation to Ottaviani et al., 2022

claim: There are widely used food composition data tables to estimate dietary intake of flavan-3-ols, (–)-epicatechin, and nitrate.
source: We used three dietary bioactives as model compounds, including ﬂavan-3-ols, (–)-epicatechin, and nitrate (Table 1) as (i) there are widely used food composition data tables used to estimate their dietary intake (Figure 1)
evidence: Statement about available food composition data, with reference to Figure 1

claim: Suitable nutritional biomarkers exist for flavan-3-ols, (–)-epicatechin, and nitrate that can provide accurate information on actual intake.
source: (ii) there exist suitable nutritional biomarkers, which can provide accurate information on actual intake Kaaks et al., 1997
evidence: Supported by citation to Kaaks et al., 1997

claim: Data from dietary intervention studies support associations between intake of flavan-3-ols, (–)-epicatechin, and nitrate and health outcomes.
source: (iii) there are data from dietary intervention studies that support associations between intake and health outcomes (Larsen et al., 2006; Ottaviani et al., 2018b; Table 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to Larsen et al., 2006 and Ottaviani et al., 2018b, and reference to Table 1

claim: The findings of this study are likely to apply to nutrients and other food constituents with high variability such as minerals.
source: While our study focuses on bioactives, it is likely that the results will also apply to nutrients and other food constituents with high variability such as minerals, where more than twofold variabilities were previously observed (Wilkinson and Perring, 1961), and other nutrients, including macronutrients such as fatty acids (Reig et al., 2013; Schwendel et al., 2015).
evidence: Inference supported by citations to Wilkinson and Perring, 1961; Reig et al., 2013; Schwendel et al., 2015

claim: Flavan-3-ols are distributed in tea, apple, and cocoa-derived products.
source: Tea, apple, and cocoa-derived products
evidence: Information from Table 1 about dietary distribution of flavan-3-ols

claim: Factors for flavan-3-ol variability include cultivar, agricultural conditions, storage, and processing.
source: Cultivar, agricultural conditions, storage, and processing
evidence: Information from Table 1 about factors affecting flavan-3-ol content

claim: Urinary concentrations of gut microbiome-derived flavan-3-ol metabolites (phenyl-γ-valerolactone metabolites) serve as biomarkers of flavan-3-ol intake.
source: Urinary concentrations of gut microbiome-derived ﬂavan-3-ol metabolites (phenyl-γ-valerolactone metabolites) (Ottaviani et al., 2018a)
evidence: Information from Table 1 supported by citation to Ottaviani et al., 2018a

claim: Flavan-3-ols reduce cardiovascular events and deaths.
source: Reduce cardiovascular events and deaths (Sesso et al., 2022. Reduce blood pressure Ottaviani et al., 2018b)
evidence: Health effect from Table 1 supported by citation to Sesso et al., 2022

claim: Flavan-3-ols reduce blood pressure.
source: Reduce cardiovascular events and deaths (Sesso et al., 2022. Reduce blood pressure Ottaviani et al., 2018b)
evidence: Health effect from Table 1 supported by citation to Ottaviani et al., 2018b

claim: Flavan-3-ols improve cognitive performance.
source: Improve cognitive performance (Sloan et al., 2021)
evidence: Health effect from Table 1 supported by citation to Sloan et al., 2021

claim: (–)-Epicatechin is distributed in tea, apple, and cocoa-derived products.
source: Tea, apple, and cocoa-derived products
evidence: Information from Table 1 about dietary distribution of (–)-epicatechin

claim: Factors for (–)-epicatechin variability include cultivar, agricultural conditions, storage, and processing (including epimerisation).
source: Cultivar, agricultural conditions, storage, and processing (including epimerisation)
evidence: Information from Table 1 about factors affecting (–)-epicatechin content

claim: Urinary concentrations of structural-related metabolites derived from phase II conjugation serve as biomarkers of (–)-epicatechin intake.
source: Urinary concentrations of structural-related metabolites derived from phase II conjugation (Ottaviani et al., 2019)
evidence: Information from Table 1 supported by citation to Ottaviani et al., 2019

claim: (–)-Epicatechin improves vascular function.
source: Improve vascular function (Schroeter et al., 2006; Dicks et al., 2022) and reduce blood pressure (Ottaviani et al., 2018b)
evidence: Health effect from Table 1 supported by citations to Schroeter et al., 2006 and Dicks et al., 2022

claim: (–)-Epicatechin reduces blood pressure.
source: Improve vascular function (Schroeter et al., 2006; Dicks et al., 2022) and reduce blood pressure (Ottaviani et al., 2018b)
evidence: Health effect from Table 1 supported by citation to Ottaviani et al., 2018b

claim: Nitrate is distributed in vegetables and drinking water.
source: Vegetables, drinking water
evidence: Information from Table 1 about dietary distribution of nitrate

claim: Nitrate content depends on a wide range of environmental factors such as fertilisation, light exposure, and water supply.
source: Depends on a wide range of environmental factors such as fertilisation, light exposure, and water supply
evidence: Information from Table 1 about factors affecting nitrate content

claim: Urinary nitrate status can be used as a surrogate marker of nitrate intake.
source: Urinary nitrate status can be used as a surrogate marker of intake (Green et al., 1981; Pannala et al., 2003; Smallwood et al., 2017)
evidence: Information from Table 1 supported by citations to Green et al., 1981; Pannala et al., 2003; Smallwood et al., 2017

claim: Dietary nitrate can reduce blood pressure.
source: Dietary nitrate can reduce blood pressure (Larsen et al., 2006)
evidence: Health effect from Table 1 supported by citation to Larsen et al., 2006

claim: The variability in bioactive content significantly contributes to the uncertainty in the estimation of dietary intake.
source: These results show that bioactive content variability signiﬁcantly contributes to the uncertainty in the estimation of dietary intake, even more than the error incurred by self-report methods that have attracted a lot of attention and discussion in nutritional research (Subar et al., 2015).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the data presented in the study, with citation to Subar et al., 2015

claim: The uncertainty associated with the use of self-reported methods is 2–25%.
source: In comparison to the uncertainty introduced by the variability in food composition, the uncertainty associated with the use of self-reported methods of 2–25% (Stubbs et al., 2014) appears to be small.
evidence: Supported by citation to Stubbs et al., 2014

claim: There is an overlap in the possible range of bioactive intake between study participants.
source: There is an overlap in the possible range of bioactive intake between study participants (Figure 2), making it diﬃcult to identify low and high consumers or to rank participants by intake (see also below).
evidence: Observation from the data shown in Figure 2

claim: Bioactive content variability makes it difficult to identify low and high consumers or to rank participants by intake.
source: There is an overlap in the possible range of bioactive intake between study participants (Figure 2), making it diﬃcult to identify low and high consumers or to rank participants by intake (see also below).
evidence: Inference drawn from the data shown in Figure 2

claim: The biomarkers used in this study have been validated and characterised previously.
source: The biomarkers used in this study (Green et al., 1981; Ottaviani et al., 2018a; Ottaviani et al., 2019; Pannala et al., 2003; Smallwood et al., 2017) have been validated and characterised previously (Table 1) and are suitable to estimate relative intake (Keogh et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Green et al., 1981; Ottaviani et al., 2018a; Ottaviani et al., 2019; Pannala et al., 2003; Smallwood et al., 2017; Keogh et al., 2013

claim: The biomarkers used in this study are suitable to estimate relative intake.
source: The biomarkers used in this study (Green et al., 1981; Ottaviani et al., 2018a; Ottaviani et al., 2019; Pannala et al., 2003; Smallwood et al., 2017) have been validated and characterised previously (Table 1) and are suitable to estimate relative intake (Keogh et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Keogh et al., 2013

claim: Only 20–30% of participants are assigned to the same quantile when comparing DD-FCT method and biomarker method.
source: The data show very modest agreement between the two measurement methods (only 20–30% of participants assigned to the same quantile) and conﬁrm that ranking is not suitable to address the measurement error and uncertainty introduced by the high variability in bioactive content.
evidence: Analysis result from comparing the two methods in the study

claim: Ranking is not suitable to address the measurement error and uncertainty introduced by the high variability in bioactive content.
source: The data show very modest agreement between the two measurement methods (only 20–30% of participants assigned to the same quantile) and conﬁrm that ranking is not suitable to address the measurement error and uncertainty introduced by the high variability in bioactive content.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the data analysis in the study

claim: Relying on a single value of bioactive content in food for all participants introduces bias when assessing relative intake of dietary compounds.
source: Overall, this shows that relying on a single value of bioactive content in food for all participants introduces bias when assessing relative intake of dietary compounds.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study results

claim: All three compounds under investigation have a well-established acute effect on vascular function.
source: We use the cross-sectional association with blood pressure as example as all three compounds have a well-established acute eﬀect on vascular function (Larsen et al., 2006; Ottaviani et al., 2018b; Schroeter et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Larsen et al., 2006; Ottaviani et al., 2018b; Schroeter et al., 2006

claim: The variability in bioactive content can result in estimated associations between intake and blood pressure ranging from beneficial to detrimental effects.
source: This is very noticeable for nitrate, where the estimated diﬀerences in blood pressure range from –1.0 (95% CI –1.6 to –0.4) mmHg between the bottom and top decile of intake, suggesting a potentially beneﬁcial, to 0.8 (0.2; 1.4) mmHg, suggesting a potentially detrimental eﬀect on health.
evidence: Data from simulations in the study

claim: Using the mean bioactive content does not resolve the challenge of obtaining reliable estimates of associations between intake and health endpoints.
source: As the actual food composition is unknown, it is not possible to obtain a reliable estimate of this association or even identify the likely direction of such an association. Using the mean bioactive content, as is common practice, does not resolve this challenge.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the simulation results in the study

claim: Biomarker-derived data show a strong and significant inverse association between intake and blood pressure.
source: Biomarker-derived data, while not deprived of limitations but certainly not aﬀected by the factors that modulate variability in food content in the DD-FCT method, show a strong and signiﬁcant inverse association between intake and blood pressure, and this association would have been missed when relying exclusively on dietary data.
evidence: Analysis result from biomarker data in the study

claim: The association between bioactive intake and blood pressure would have been missed when relying exclusively on dietary data.
source: Biomarker-derived data, while not deprived of limitations but certainly not aﬀected by the factors that modulate variability in food content in the DD-FCT method, show a strong and signiﬁcant inverse association between intake and blood pressure, and this association would have been missed when relying exclusively on dietary data.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparing biomarker and dietary data results

claim: The variability in bioactive content can impact the estimated associations between the DD-FCT method intake assessments and health endpoints.
source: These results show that the variability in bioactive content can impact the estimated associations between the DD-FCT method intake assessments and health endpoints.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study results

claim: Even when using the same food intake data, differences in bioactive content can result in diametrically opposite results.
source: It demonstrates that even when using the self-same food intake data, diﬀerences in bioactive content can result in diametrically opposite results.
evidence: Observation from the simulation results in the study

claim: Many reported associations between bioactive intake and health are likely unreliable because most studies do not take variability in food composition into account.
source: Considering that most studies investigating the associations between the intake of bioactives and health do not take variability in food composition into account, it is likely that many reported associations are unreliable.
evidence: Inference drawn from the study findings applied to the broader literature

claim: The variability in food composition represents a significant factor that needs to be taken into consideration in nutrition research.
source: In this study, we investigated how the variability in food composition aﬀects nutritional research. Our results, based on three bioactives, show that the variability in food composition represents a signiﬁcant factor that needs to be taken into consideration.
evidence: Main conclusion from the study results

claim: The use of single-point estimates of food composition data represents a significant oversimplification that yields unreliable data.
source: The use of single-point estimates of food composition data represents a signiﬁcant oversimpliﬁcation that yields unreliable data as the actual intake can be considerably diﬀerent from the estimated intake.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study results

claim: The variability in food composition makes reliable estimates of both absolute and relative intake of bioactives challenging and potentially highly unreliable when solely relying on a combination of self-reported dietary data and food composition databases.
source: Our results show that the variability in food composition makes reliable estimates of both absolute and relative intake of bioactives challenging and potentially highly unreliable when solely relying on a combination of self-reported dietary data and food composition databases.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study results

claim: Any associations between intake and health outcomes derived from using many current approaches are unreliable.
source: This signiﬁcant limitation is further applied by the bias introduced through limitations of dietary assessment itself (e.g., reporting bias). Thus, any associations between intake and health outcomes derived from using many current approaches are unreliable.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study findings

claim: For the three food constituents under investigation, a Janus-like effect was found with negative and positive associations using the same food consumption data and food content within the reported range.
source: Indeed, for the three food constituents under investigation, we found a Janus-like eﬀect with negative and positive associations using the self-same food consumption data and food content within the reported range.
evidence: Result from the study simulations

claim: The variability in food composition might help explain why nutritional advice given to the general public can feel inconstant and contradictory.
source: This might help explain why nutritional advice given to the general public can feel inconstant, and even contradictory, at times, especially when observing the evolution of advisory statements on the same foods, food groups, or nutrients over time.
evidence: Speculative inference drawn from the study findings

claim: Validated nutritional biomarkers can provide a reliable estimate of nutrient and bioactive intake as they are based on their systemic presence and do not rely on assumptions about food composition data.
source: Validated nutritional biomarkers, especially recovery biomarkers (Kaaks et al., 1997), can provide a reliable estimate of nutrient and bioactive intake as they are based on their systemic presence and do not rely on assumptions about food composition data.
evidence: Statement about biomarker advantages, supported by citation to Kaaks et al., 1997

claim: Biomarkers provide better information to investigate the associations between intake and health biomarkers as they reflect not just consumption but also nutrient–nutrient interactions and bioavailability.
source: In contrast to the duplicate diet method, which relies on the full analysis of all foods consumed, biomarkers provide better information to investigate the associations between intake and health biomarkers as they reﬂect not just consumption but also nutrient–nutrient interactions and bioavailability, which can aﬀect the systemic presence of many bioactives (Ottaviani et al., 2023).
evidence: Statement about biomarker advantages, supported by citation to Ottaviani et al., 2023

claim: The limitations of biomarker-based methods can be addressed today and often deliver greater overall improvements than addressing the limitations of non-biomarker-based approaches.
source: The application of biomarkers to assess nutrient intakes is not without limitations; however, these limitations can be addressed today. Doing so is often of greater technical feasibility and tenably delivers greater overall improvements than to address the limitations of current non-biomarker-based approaches, including self-report bias and the imprecisions and other limitations of today's food composition databases.
evidence: Argument about the relative advantages of biomarker-based approaches

claim: Successfully mitigating limitations related to reporting bias and food composition analyses does not address the inherent shortfalls of non-biomarker-based methods.
source: This is due to the fact that even successfully mitigating limitations related to reporting bias and food composition analyses does not address the inherent shortfalls of non-biomarker-based methods.
evidence: Logical argument about the limitations of non-biomarker methods

claim: An important challenge when developing biomarker-based methods is related to the inter-subject variance in the absorption and metabolism of a specific nutrient or bioactive.
source: An important challenge when developing biomarker-based methods for assessing intake is related to the inter-subject variance in the absorption and metabolism of a speciﬁc nutrient or bioactive.
evidence: Statement about challenges in biomarker development based on knowledge

claim: It is important to establish a physiological link as well as a strong statistical association between intake and biomarker.
source: It is therefore important to establish a physiological link as well as a strong statistical association between intake and biomarker, such as has been done for the biomarkers used in this study (Ottaviani et al., 2018a; Ottaviani et al., 2019; Pannala et al., 2003).
evidence: Statement about biomarker validation requirements, with citations to Ottaviani et al., 2018a; Ottaviani et al., 2019; Pannala et al., 2003

claim: Biomarkers need to be evaluated using data of actual bioactive intake and should not rely on published food composition data.
source: Biomarkers need to be evaluated using data of actual bioactive intake and should not rely on published food composition data due to the limitations described above.
evidence: Recommendation based on the study findings

claim: Biomarker-based ranking of intake is much more reliable than the rankings based on methods relying on self-reported data and food composition databases.
source: Our results however show that biomarker-based ranking of intake is much more reliable than the rankings based on methods relying on self-reported data and food composition databases.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study results

claim: High variability in food composition has been described for a range of compounds, including the fatty acid composition of dairy.
source: High variability in food composition has been described for a range of compounds, for example, for the fatty acid composition of dairy (Moate et al., 2007; Stergiadis et al., 2019) or vitamins (Phillips et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Moate et al., 2007 and Stergiadis et al., 2019

claim: High variability in food composition has been described for vitamins.
source: High variability in food composition has been described for a range of compounds, for example, for the fatty acid composition of dairy (Moate et al., 2007; Stergiadis et al., 2019) or vitamins (Phillips et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Phillips et al., 2018

claim: There is longitudinal variation in food composition, in particular due to changes to cultivars, production practices, and distribution and processing methods.
source: There is also a longitudinal variation in food composition, in particular due to changes to cultivars, production practices, and distribution and processing methods (Davis et al., 2004), and climate change is likely to exaggerate this (Macdiarmid and Whybrow, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Davis et al., 2004 and Macdiarmid and Whybrow, 2019

claim: Climate change is likely to exaggerate longitudinal variation in food composition.
source: There is also a longitudinal variation in food composition, in particular due to changes to cultivars, production practices, and distribution and processing methods (Davis et al., 2004), and climate change is likely to exaggerate this (Macdiarmid and Whybrow, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Macdiarmid and Whybrow, 2019

claim: Bioactive and nutrient content variability must be taken into consideration when choosing the tools to investigate not only dietary bioactives but also micro- and macronutrients.
source: Thus, bioactive and nutrient content variability must be taken into consideration when choosing the tools to investigate not only dietary bioactives but also micro- and macronutrients.
evidence: Recommendation based on the study findings

claim: Methods commonly used to address measurement error in nutritional research, such as regression calibration, are not suitable to address the limitations introduced by the high variability.
source: The methods commonly used to address measurement error in nutritional research, such as regression calibration (Spiegelman et al., 1997), are not suitable to address the limitations introduced by the high variabilty.
evidence: Statement about limitations of current methods, with citation to Spiegelman et al., 1997

claim: The composition of the food actually consumed by participants is impossible to predict as it depends on a range of factors, many of which are unknown to consumers and researchers.
source: However, the composition of the food actually consumed by participants is impossible to predict as it depends on a range of factors, many of which are unknown to consumers and researchers as outlined in the introduction.
evidence: Logical argument based on the factors discussed in the introduction

claim: The study excluded other sources of bias and variability by using the same dietary data for all analyses using only acute intake data and an endpoint that is affected directly by intake.
source: We excluded those from our study as much as possible by using the self-same dietary data for all analyses using only acute intake data (24 hr dietary recall and spot urine samples) and an endpoint that is aﬀected directly by intake.
evidence: Description of the study design

claim: The study design allows attribution of findings mainly to the variability in food composition.
source: This allows us to attribute our ﬁndings mainly to the variability in food composition.
evidence: Inference about the study design's ability to isolate the effect of food composition variability

claim: The study used measures of acute intake (24 hr dietary recalls and spot urine samples) and used a health endpoint that is directly affected by intake.
source: We also used measures of acute intake (24 hr dietary recalls and spot urine samples) and used a health endpoint that is directly aﬀected by intake.
evidence: Description of the study methodology

claim: It is expected that the variability in food composition affects prospective analyses more than cross-sectional analyses.
source: It is expected that the variability in food composition aﬀects prospective analyses more than cross-sectional analyses: in addition to the variability in food content, the composition of foods changes over time (Davis et al., 2004; White and Broadley, 2005).
evidence: Speculation supported by citations to Davis et al., 2004 and White and Broadley, 2005

claim: The composition of foods changes over time.
source: It is expected that the variability in food composition aﬀects prospective analyses more than cross-sectional analyses: in addition to the variability in food content, the composition of foods changes over time (Davis et al., 2004; White and Broadley, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Davis et al., 2004 and White and Broadley, 2005

claim: The content of proline-betaine in citrus fruits is highly variable (14.3—110 mg/100 mL in various citrus fruit juice).
source: A number of biomarkers have been proposed to estimate the intake of individual foods, for example, proline-betaine as biomarker of citrus fruit intake (Gibbons et al., 2017), but the content in citrus fruits is highly variable (14.3—110 mg/100 mL in various citrus fruit juice; Lang et al., 2017), and it is thus not possible to estimate actual food intake without using foods in which the content of the dietary compound to use as a biomarker is standardised.
evidence: Supported by citations to Gibbons et al., 2017 and Lang et al., 2017

claim: It is not possible to estimate actual food intake without using foods in which the content of the dietary compound to use as a biomarker is standardised.
source: A number of biomarkers have been proposed to estimate the intake of individual foods, for example, proline-betaine as biomarker of citrus fruit intake (Gibbons et al., 2017), but the content in citrus fruits is highly variable (14.3—110 mg/100 mL in various citrus fruit juice; Lang et al., 2017), and it is thus not possible to estimate actual food intake without using foods in which the content of the dietary compound to use as a biomarker is standardised.
evidence: Inference drawn from the variability data

claim: Changes in the composition of foods affect the concentration of metabolites and thereby reduce the reliability of metabolite-based biomarkers of individual foods or dietary pattern.
source: They are usually developed under highly standardised conditions and reﬂect the composition of the foods consumed during these studies. Changes in the composition of these foods aﬀect the concentration of metabolites and thereby reduce the reliability of metabolite-based biomarkers of individual foods or dietary pattern.
evidence: Logical inference about the effect of food composition changes on metabolite biomarkers

claim: The limitations of metabolite-based biomarkers diminish their suitability for longitudinal or multicentre studies where a high variability in food composition is likely.
source: This diminishes the suitability of such markers for longitudinal or multicentre studies where a high variability in food composition is likely.
evidence: Inference about the applicability of metabolite biomarkers

claim: The limitations of metabolite-based biomarkers do not apply to the development of biomarkers of specific bioactives or other nutrients as the variability of bioactive and nutrient content is reflected in the variation of biomarker levels.
source: These limitations do not apply to the development of biomarkers of speciﬁc bioactives or other nutrients as the variability of bioactive and nutrient content is reﬂected in the variation of biomarker levels.
evidence: Logical argument about the difference between food-based and nutrient-based biomarkers

claim: The data clearly show that the results based on the DD-FCT method are likely to be biased and unreliable.
source: Our data clearly show that the results based on the DD-FCT method are likely to be biased and unreliable.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study results

claim: Dietary recommendations based on data from the DD-FCT method are likely to be unreliable and misleading.
source: Dietary recommendation based on such data emanating from that approach are therefore also likely to be unreliable and misleading.
evidence: Inference drawn from the unreliability of DD-FCT method results

claim: The high variability in food composition has an impact on the translation of health-based guidance values into food-based dietary recommendations.
source: However, the high variability in food composition also has an impact on the translation of health-based guidance values into food-based dietary recommendations.
evidence: Logical inference about the implications of food composition variability

claim: The amount of flavan-3-ols required to achieve a vasculoprotective effect according to the EFSA health claim is 200 mg/day.
source: For example, the amount of ﬂavan-3-ols required to achieve a vasculoprotective eﬀect according to the EFSA health claim is 200 mg/day (EFSA Panel on Dietetic Products, Nutrition and Allergies, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to EFSA Panel on Dietetic Products, Nutrition and Allergies, 2014

claim: When using mean food composition data, 200 mg/day of flavan-3-ols could be achieved by five cups of tea.
source: When using mean food composition data (Rothwell et al., 2013), this could be achieved by five cups of tea.
evidence: Calculation based on food composition data from Rothwell et al., 2013

claim: When using the lowest reported food content, at least 22 cups of tea would have to be consumed to meet the recommended intake of 200 mg/day flavan-3-ols.
source: However, when using the lowest reported food content, at least 22 cups of tea would have to be consumed to meet the recommended intake.
evidence: Calculation based on minimum food content data

claim: 5–6 apples would be sufficient to consume the 50 mg/day (–)-epicatechin assumed to be sufficient to improve vascular function when using mean food content.
source: Similarly, 5–6 apples would be suﬃcient to consume the 50 mg/day (–)-epicatechin assumed to be suﬃcient to improve vascular function (Ellinger et al., 2012; Hooper et al., 2012) when using mean food content, but it could be up to 27 when assuming a low content in food.
evidence: Calculation based on food composition data, with citations to Ellinger et al., 2012 and Hooper et al., 2012

claim: Up to 27 apples could be required to consume 50 mg/day (–)-epicatechin when assuming a low content in food.
source: Similarly, 5–6 apples would be suﬃcient to consume the 50 mg/day (–)-epicatechin assumed to be suﬃcient to improve vascular function (Ellinger et al., 2012; Hooper et al., 2012) when using mean food content, but it could be up to 27 when assuming a low content in food.
evidence: Calculation based on minimum food content data

claim: It would not be possible to determine whether or not a population is already meeting dietary recommendation for flavan-3-ols without the development of biomarker-based methods.
source: In this manner, it would not be possible to determine whether or not a population is already meeting dietary recommendation for ﬂavan-3-ols without the development of biomarker-based methods (Crowe-White et al., 2022).
evidence: Inference supported by citation to Crowe-White et al., 2022

claim: The findings have an impact on the risk assessment of food components that are naturally present in foods and used as additives such as nitrates.
source: These ﬁndings also have an impact on the risk assessment of food components, in particular those that are naturally present in foods and used as additives such as nitrates (Mortensen et al., 2017) or phosphates (Younes et al., 2019).
evidence: Inference supported by citations to Mortensen et al., 2017 and Younes et al., 2019

claim: Results from observational studies and intervention studies relying on food content data will be affected by inaccurate assessment of intake.
source: Results from observational studies and intervention studies relying on food content data will be aﬀected by inaccurate assessment of intake as described above.
evidence: Inference drawn from the study findings

claim: The exposure assessment in risk assessment will be affected by the variability of data, with consequences for consumers and food producers.
source: More importantly, however, the exposure assessment will be aﬀected by the variability of data, with consequences for consumers and food producers as an overestimation of exposure could result in unnecessary restrictions in use, whereas an underestimation could put consumers at risk.
evidence: Logical inference about the implications of variability in exposure assessment

claim: The ADI (acceptable daily intake) for nitrate is 3.7 mg/kg BW/day.
source: For example, in EPIC Norfolk, none or only a very few study participants exceed the ADI (acceptable daily intake) of 3.7 mg/kg BW/day (Mortensen et al., 2017) for nitrate when estimating intake with minimum and mean food content, respectively.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mortensen et al., 2017

claim: In EPIC Norfolk, none or only a very few study participants exceed the ADI for nitrate when estimating intake with minimum and mean food content.
source: For example, in EPIC Norfolk, none or only a very few study participants exceed the ADI (acceptable daily intake) of 3.7 mg/kg BW/day (Mortensen et al., 2017) for nitrate when estimating intake with minimum and mean food content, respectively.
evidence: Analysis result from the study data

claim: When using the maximum food content, one-third of EPIC Norfolk study participants exceed the ADI for nitrate.
source: However, when using the maximum food content, one-third of study participants exceed the ADI for nitrate, and almost 10% exceed it twofold.
evidence: Analysis result from the study data

claim: When using the maximum food content, almost 10% of EPIC Norfolk study participants exceed the ADI for nitrate twofold.
source: However, when using the maximum food content, one-third of study participants exceed the ADI for nitrate, and almost 10% exceed it twofold.
evidence: Analysis result from the study data

claim: Different scenarios of nitrate intake would result in very different actions by risk managers due to the different impact on population health.
source: Each of these scenarios would result in very diﬀerent actions by risk managers due to the diﬀerent impact on population health, and in the latter case more stringent restrictions were necessary.
evidence: Inference about the implications for risk management

claim: The results of many interventional and observational nutrition studies using dietary surveys in combination with food composition data are potentially unreliable and carry greater limitations than commonly appreciated.
source: Our data suggest that the results of many interventional and observational nutrition studies using dietary surveys in combination with food composition data are potentially unreliable and carry greater limitations than commonly appreciated.
evidence: Main conclusion drawn from the study results

claim: Studies using food composition data are used to derive evidence-based dietary recommendations and disease risk assessments.
source: As these studies are used to derive evidence-based dietary recommendations and disease risk assessments, their limitations could have a considerable impact on public health.
evidence: Statement about the use of nutrition studies based on knowledge

claim: The limitations of studies using food composition data could have a considerable impact on public health.
source: As these studies are used to derive evidence-based dietary recommendations and disease risk assessments, their limitations could have a considerable impact on public health.
evidence: Inference about the implications of study limitations

claim: Results relying solely on food composition data not only failed to identify beneficial associations between three bioactives and blood pressure, but even suggested possible adverse associations.
source: We demonstrated that the results relying solely on food composition data not only failed to identify beneﬁcial associations between three bioactives and blood pressure, but even suggested possible adverse associations.
evidence: Summary of the study findings

claim: It is highly likely that the findings of this nature are not limited to the model compounds but broadly apply to other dietary components as well.
source: It is highly likely that the ﬁndings of this nature are not limited to the model compounds that served as examples in our investigation here but broadly apply to other dietary components as well.
evidence: Inference about the generalizability of the findings

claim: It is crucial to address the limitation of food composition variability by revisiting previous studies and by taking these limitations into consideration in future studies.
source: Given the importance of diet in the maintenance of health and disease risk reduction, it is crucial to address this limitation: both by revisiting previous studies and by taking these limitations into consideration in future studies.
evidence: Recommendation based on the study findings

claim: It is essential to develop and use nutritional biomarkers to determine actual nutrient intakes that ensure more reliable and actionable insights.
source: We think it is essential to develop and use nutritional biomarkers to determine actual nutrient intakes that ensure more reliable and actionable insights.
evidence: Recommendation based on the study findings

claim: The development of more and better biomarkers for accurate dietary assessment remains crucial.
source: This means that the development of more and better biomarkers for accurate dietary assessment remains crucial (Prentice, 2018).
evidence: Recommendation supported by citation to Prentice, 2018

claim: The technical capabilities required for developing biomarker-based approaches are broadly available today.
source: The challenges associated with developing biomarker-based approaches are not insigniﬁcant, but the technical capabilities required are broadly available today, and the advantages of deploying improved approaches to establishing the links between diet and health are so signiﬁcant, timely, and needed that it should become a standard tool in nutrition research.
evidence: Statement about current technical capabilities

claim: Biomarker-based approaches should become a standard tool in nutrition research.
source: The challenges associated with developing biomarker-based approaches are not insigniﬁcant, but the technical capabilities required are broadly available today, and the advantages of deploying improved approaches to establishing the links between diet and health are so signiﬁcant, timely, and needed that it should become a standard tool in nutrition research.
evidence: Recommendation based on the study findings and assessment of current capabilities

claim: Between 1993 and 1997, 30,447 women and men aged between 40 and 79 years were recruited for the Norfolk cohort of the EPIC study.
source: Between 1993 and 1997, 30,447 women and men aged between 40 and 79 years were recruited for the Norfolk cohort of the EPIC study, and 25,639 attended a health examination (Day et al., 1999).
evidence: Description of the study population, supported by citation to Day et al., 1999

claim: 25,639 participants attended a health examination in the EPIC Norfolk study.
source: Between 1993 and 1997, 30,447 women and men aged between 40 and 79 years were recruited for the Norfolk cohort of the EPIC study, and 25,639 attended a health examination (Day et al., 1999).
evidence: Description of the study population, supported by citation to Day et al., 1999

claim: The study was approved by the Norwich Local Research Ethics Committee.
source: The study was approved by the Norwich Local Research Ethics Committee, all participants gave written, informed consent, and all methods were carried out in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations.
evidence: Statement about ethical approval

claim: All participants gave written, informed consent.
source: The study was approved by the Norwich Local Research Ethics Committee, all participants gave written, informed consent, and all methods were carried out in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations.
evidence: Statement about informed consent

claim: Diet was assessed by 7-day diary (7DD), whereby the first day of the diary was completed as a 24 hr recall (24HDR) with a trained interviewer.
source: Diet was assessed by 7-day diary (7DD), whereby the ﬁrst day of the diary was completed as a 24 hr recall (24HDR) with a trained interviewer and the remainder completed during subsequent days.
evidence: Description of the dietary assessment method

claim: Flavan-3-ol intake was estimated as the sum of epicatechin, catechin, epicatechin-3-O-gallate, catechin-3-O-gallate, and proanthocyanidins.
source: Flavan-3-ol intake (the sum of epicatechin, catechin, epicatechin-3-O-gallate, catechin-3-O-gallate, and proanthocyanidins) was estimated as described previously Vogiatzoglou et al., 2015
evidence: Description of the intake estimation method, with citation to Vogiatzoglou et al., 2015

claim: gVLMB includes the metabolites 5-(4′-hydroxyphenyl)-γ-valerolactone-3′-glucuronide (gVL3G) and 5-(4′-hydroxyphenyl)-γ-valerolactone-3′-sulphate (gVL3S).
source: We used two diﬀerent biomarkers to estimate ﬂavan-3-ol and (–)-epicatechin intake: gVLMB that includes the metabolites 5-(4′-hydroxyphenyl)-γ-valerolactone-3′-glucuronide (gVL3G) and 5-(4′-hydroxyphenyl)-γ-valerolactone-3′-sulphate (gVL3S)
evidence: Description of the biomarker composition

claim: SREMB includes the metabolites (–)-epicatechin-3′-glucuronide (E3G), (–)-epicatechin-3′-sulphate (E3S) and 3′-methoxy(–)-epicatechin-5-sulphate (3Me5S).
source: SREMB that includes the metabolites (–)-epicatechin-3′-glucuronide (E3G), (–)-epicatechin-3′-sulphate (E3S) and 3′-methoxy(–)-epicatechin-5-sulphate (3Me5S).
evidence: Description of the biomarker composition

claim: gVLMB are specific for estimating the intake of flavan-3-ols in general, including (±)-epicatechin, (±)-catechin, (±)-epicatechin-3-O-gallate, (±)-catechin-3-O-gallate, and procyanidins.
source: gVLMB are speciﬁc for estimating the intake of ﬂavan-3-ols in general, including (±)-epicatechin, (±)-catechin, (±)-epicatechin-3-O-gallate, (±)-catechin-3-O-gallate, and procyanidins and excluding the ﬂavan-3-ols gallocatechin, epigallocatechin, gallocatechin-3-O-gallate, epigallocatechin-3-O-gallate, theaﬂavins, and thearubigins (Ottaviani et al., 2018a).
evidence: Description of biomarker specificity, supported by citation to Ottaviani et al., 2018a

claim: gVLMB exclude the flavan-3-ols gallocatechin, epigallocatechin, gallocatechin-3-O-gallate, epigallocatechin-3-O-gallate, theaflavins, and thearubigins.
source: gVLMB are speciﬁc for estimating the intake of ﬂavan-3-ols in general, including (±)-epicatechin, (±)-catechin, (±)-epicatechin-3-O-gallate, (±)-catechin-3-O-gallate, and procyanidins and excluding the ﬂavan-3-ols gallocatechin, epigallocatechin, gallocatechin-3-O-gallate, epigallocatechin-3-O-gallate, theaﬂavins, and thearubigins (Ottaviani et al., 2018a).
evidence: Description of biomarker specificity, supported by citation to Ottaviani et al., 2018a

claim: SREMB are specific for (–)-epicatechin intake.
source: SREMB are speciﬁc for (–)-epicatechin intake (Ottaviani et al., 2019).
evidence: Description of biomarker specificity, supported by citation to Ottaviani et al., 2019

claim: Stability analyses confirmed that biomarkers are stable under the storage conditions used.
source: Spot urine samples were collected during the baseline health examination and stored in glass bottles at –20°C until analysis. Stability analyses conﬁrmed that biomarkers are stable under these conditions (Ottaviani et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ottaviani et al., 2019

claim: The lower limit of quantification (LLOQ) for the biomarker analysis was 0.1 μM.
source: Concentrations below the lower limit of quantiﬁcation (LLOQ, 0.1 μM) were used for the analysis to avoid the bias of substituting a range of values by a single value.
evidence: Description of the analytical method

claim: Concentrations were adjusted by specific gravity for dilution as the endpoint of the analysis, systolic blood pressure, was strongly correlated with urinary creatinine.
source: Concentrations were adjusted by speciﬁc gravity for dilution as the endpoint of the analysis, systolic blood pressure, was strongly correlated with urinary creatinine.
evidence: Description of the data adjustment method and rationale

claim: Between 50 and 80% of dietary nitrate are recovered in urine.
source: Urinary nitrate concentration, adjusted for dilution by speciﬁc gravity, was used as a biomarker of nitrate intake, as between 50 and 80% of dietary nitrate are recovered in urine, whereas endogenous production is relatively stable at 0.57 (95% CI 0.27–0.86) mmol/day (Green et al., 1981; Packer et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to Green et al., 1981 and Packer et al., 1989

claim: Endogenous nitrate production is relatively stable at 0.57 (95% CI 0.27–0.86) mmol/day.
source: Urinary nitrate concentration, adjusted for dilution by speciﬁc gravity, was used as a biomarker of nitrate intake, as between 50 and 80% of dietary nitrate are recovered in urine, whereas endogenous production is relatively stable at 0.57 (95% CI 0.27–0.86) mmol/day (Green et al., 1981; Packer et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to Green et al., 1981 and Packer et al., 1989

claim: 10,000 simulations were conducted to explore the impact of the variability on bioactive content.
source: We conducted 10,000 simulations to explore the impact of the variability on bioactive content.
evidence: Description of the simulation methodology

claim: A uniform distribution was assumed for food composition as the data available do not suggest that food composition follows a normal distribution.
source: The data available do not suggest that food composition follows a normal distribution, and we therefore assumed a uniform distribution.
evidence: Description of the statistical assumption made in the analysis

claim: Biomarker data were positively skewed (log-normal distribution), and therefore log2-transformed data were used for all analyses.
source: Biomarker data were positively skewed (log-normal distribution), and, therefore, log2-transformed data were used for all analyses.
evidence: Description of the data transformation method

claim: Restricted cubic splines (3 knots, outer quantiles 0.1 and 0.9) were used for all continuous variables unless indicated otherwise.
source: Restricted cubic splines (3 knots, outer quantiles 0.1 and 0.9; using the rcs function; Harrell, 2023) were used for all continuous variables unless indicated otherwise.
evidence: Description of the statistical method, with citation to Harrell, 2023

claim: Cross-sectional analyses were stratified by sex.
source: In cross-sectional analyses, stratiﬁed by sex, we investigated the associations between biomarker and 24 hr recall estimated ﬂavan-3-ol, (–)-epicatechin, and nitrate intake (biomarkers adjusted by speciﬁc gravity adjusted, dietary data by energy, log2-transformed), as independent variable and systolic and diastolic blood pressure (mmHg) using multiple regression analyses.
evidence: Description of the analysis approach

claim: Analyses were adjusted by age, body mass index, plasma vitamin C, smoking status, physical activity, and health at baseline.
source: Analyses were adjusted by age (continuous; years), body mass index (BMI) (continuous, kg/m2), plasma vitamin C, smoking status (categorical; never, ever, former), physical activity (categorical; inactive, moderately inactive, moderately active, active), and health at baseline (self-reported diabetes mellitus, myocardial infarction, cerebrovascular accident).
evidence: Description of the statistical adjustment
